lines.text: More than seven thousand islands, three centuries of Spain, half a century of America, and a people who toppled a dictator without firing a shot. This is the Philippines.
Long before any outsider came, the Ifugao people carved rice terraces up the steep mountains of Luzon, like giant green stairs.
On the island of Mactan lived a chief named Lapulapu. One day he would become the first Filipino hero.
In 1519 a Spanish fleet under Magellan set out to reach the Spice Islands by sailing west. Its path led straight to these islands.
In 1521, on Mactan, Lapulapu's warriors met the newcomers and killed Magellan. One ship sailed on, and finished the first voyage around the world.
Spain came back to stay. For two hundred and fifty years, great galleons carried silver and silk between Manila and Mexico.
In 1571 the Spanish founded Manila on its wide bay, the capital of a colony that would become largely Catholic.
Three centuries on, the doctor and writer Jose Rizal wrote novels that laid bare Spanish rule. His execution in 1896 helped spark a revolution.
Andres Bonifacio founded the Katipunan, the secret society that took up arms against Spain.
Emilio Aguinaldo, a young general, would lead the fight and become the nation's first president.
In 1896 the revolution began, and spread across the islands.
By 1898 a new nation had declared itself, the Philippines, a mix of Asian and Spanish heritage.
On the twelfth of June 1898, Aguinaldo proclaimed independence from Spain. The day is still celebrated.
But Spain had sold the islands to the United States, and in a bitter war, America crushed the young republic.
Ferdinand Marcos would rise to the presidency in 1965, and hold on to it for over twenty years.
Corazon Aquino would one day lead the movement that ended his rule.
In the Second World War Japan invaded. In 1942 tens of thousands of American and Filipino prisoners were forced to march, and thousands died.
In October 1944 American forces landed on Leyte, and off its coast the Japanese fleet was crushed, in what is often called the largest naval battle ever.
Rodrigo Duterte would be elected president in 2016, and wage a war on drugs that killed thousands.
And Bongbong Marcos, the dictator's son, would one day win the presidency himself.
Independent since 1946, the country faced a dark turn in 1972, when Marcos declared martial law and ruled by decree.
In 1975 the world watched Manila, as Muhammad Ali and Joe Frazier fought their last, brutal bout in the tropical heat.
Boxing would bring the country another legend, Manny Pacquiao, a world champion in eight weight classes.
In February 1986 millions filled the streets, peacefully, and Marcos fled. People Power had won.
In 1991 Mount Pinatubo exploded, one of the century's largest eruptions. Warnings saved thousands, and its ash cooled the whole planet for a while.
In 2013 Typhoon Haiyan tore through the central islands, killing more than six thousand people.
And in 2025 the former president Duterte was arrested on a warrant of the International Criminal Court.
Through conquest, war and storms, the people of these islands have kept writing their own story.
